title: Naive Interactive Session Logging (Shell Command Auditing Bypass)
pattern: Relying on high-level command shells or file-system-level command tracking (like `.bash_history` or standard output transcripts) to provide robust administrative session auditing.
why_bad: Interactive auditing is trivial to bypass. An attacker can start a shell, open an editor (like `vim`), and execute arbitrary shell commands from within the editor (e.g., `:!/bin/evilcmd`). This bypasses history logs entirely and muddled standard transcripts with terminal control characters.
detection: Relying on standard user-mode shell logs or command-logging wrappers on boundaries where strict administrative security accountability is claimed.
fix: Enforce low-level kernel auditing (like system-call capture) or restrict administrative tasks to small, granular functional API proxies that log the specific request instead of raw shell sessions.
source: `Heather Adkins et al. - Building Secure and Reliable Systems (2020)`, Ch 5, p. 66.
